(CNN) -- The Sri Lankan army launched an operation against Tamil rebels in the country's north early Monday, the military said, claiming to have rescued thousands of civilians trapped in a government safe zone. The Sri Lankan army has relaunched its attacks on Tamil rebels in the country's north. A rebel Web site, TamilNet, said government forces were engaged in a fresh ground offensive. A TamilNet correspondent in Vanni reported heavy shelling, rocket fire and gunfire. Thirty civilians died in shelling Sunday, rebels said. The government of Sri Lanka has been battling the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Elam (LTTE) rebels in a civil conflict that has lasted nearly 25 years. "Thousands of civilians who had been forcibly held by the LTTE terrorists in the government declared No Fire Zone (NFZ) were rescued early hours this morning, 20 April, as the troops engaged in a massive scale rescue mission, were able to open a safe passage for the civilians," the Ministry of Defense Web site said. More than 10,000 civilians are trying to seek refuge with soldiers, the military said. The upsurge in hostilities follows a two-day cessation last week for the Sinhala and Hindu New Year. The U.S. State Department on Thursday called for a cease-fire between the Sri Lankan government and Tamil Tigers to allow civilians to escape the fighting. "We call upon the government and military of Sri Lanka, and the Tamil Tigers, to immediately stop hostilities until the more than 140,000 civilians in the conflict area are safely out," acting spokesman Robert Wood said in a statement. "Both sides must immediately return to a humanitarian pause and both must respect the right of free movement of those civilian men, women and children trapped by the fighting."  Watch the heavy toll of fighting on civilians » . A brief cessation of hostilities  announced by the Sri Lankan government on April 12 allowed the United Nations and its partners to bring in aid, but a renewed government offensive has left civilians trapped in a war zone. U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and his humanitarian chief John Holmes called the brief halt in fighting inadequate and have pushed for a longer humanitarian pause in fighting. The most pressing concern now, according to Holmes, is the fact that more than 100,000 people are crowded in a "very small pocket of land" that is about five square miles, or about twice the size of New York's Central Park. "It is a very small area indeed for what we believe is a very large number of people," Holmes told reporters Wednesday. Overcrowding is also a problem in camps housing displaced people, according to the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). As of Monday, some 65,000 displaced people were crammed into camps in Vavuniya, Jaffna and Mannar, with 35,000 more expected to arrive within 48 hours, the organization said in a statement. ' UNICEF said it feared for children trapped in the escalating fighting and is worried that the worst is yet to come. The group appealed for donations to help cover "the most immediate needs of the affected population in health and nutrition, water and sanitation, protection and education." The crowded population, primarily comprised of Tamil civilians, is subject to the continuing Sri Lankan government assaults. The British and French foreign ministers released a joint statement as well on Wednesday, saying that the Tamil Tigers are using Tamil civilians as human shields. The Tigers have been declared a terrorist organization by 32 countries, including the United States and the European Union. As many as 70,000 people have been killed since the conflict officially began in 1983. The International Committee of the Red Cross said Monday that it has helped evacuate more than 10,000 sick and injured patients, and their caregivers, from Putumattalan in rebel-held territory since February. "These evacuations have saved many lives," said Morven Murchinson, the Red Cross medical coordinator in Sri Lanka. "It is vital that they continue, because more sick and wounded people are arriving every day at the makeshift medical facilities in Putumattalan." The Red Cross says there's an acute shortage of medical supplies in the region, which it is trying to rectify.

The Sri Lankan army has relaunched attacks on Tamil rebels in the country’s north. TamilNet, a rebel Web site, reported that government forces were engaged in a fresh ground offensive. A TamilNet correspondent in Vanni described heavy shelling, rocket fire and gunfire. Rebels said 30 civilians were killed in shelling Sunday.

The government of Sri Lanka has been battling the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Elam (LTTE) rebels in a civil conflict that has lasted nearly 25 years.

“Thousands of civilians who had been forcibly held by the LTTE terrorists in the government declared No Fire Zone (NFZ) were rescued early hours this morning, 20 April, as the troops engaged in a massive scale rescue mission, were able to open a safe passage for the civilians,” the Ministry of Defense Web site said.

More than 10,000 civilians are attempting to seek refuge with soldiers, the military said.

The upsurge in hostilities follows a two-day cessation last week for the Sinhala and Hindu New Year. On Thursday, the U.S. State Department called for a cease-fire between the Sri Lankan government and the Tamil Tigers to allow civilians to escape the fighting.

“We call upon the government and military of Sri Lanka, and the Tamil Tigers, to immediately stop hostilities until the more than 140,000 civilians in the conflict area are safely out,” acting spokesman Robert Wood said in a statement. “Both sides must immediately return to a humanitarian pause and both must respect the right of free movement of those civilian men, women and children trapped by the fighting.”

Watch the heavy toll of fighting on civilians »

A brief cessation of hostilities announced by the Sri Lankan government on April 12 allowed the United Nations and its partners to bring in aid, but a renewed government offensive has left civilians trapped in a war zone.

U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and his humanitarian chief, John Holmes, called the brief halt in fighting inadequate and have pressed for a longer humanitarian pause.

According to Holmes, the most pressing concern is that more than 100,000 people are crowded into a “very small pocket of land” of about five square miles, roughly twice the size of New York’s Central Park.

“It is a very small area indeed for what we believe is a very large number of people,” Holmes told reporters Wednesday.

Overcrowding is also a problem in camps housing displaced people, according to the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF). As of Monday, some 65,000 displaced people were crammed into camps in Vavuniya, Jaffna and Mannar, with 35,000 more expected to arrive within 48 hours, the organization said in a statement.

UNICEF said it feared for children trapped in the escalating fighting and was concerned that the worst was yet to come. The group appealed for donations to help cover “the most immediate needs of the affected population in health and nutrition, water and sanitation, protection and education.”

The crowded population, primarily composed of Tamil civilians, remains subject to continuing Sri Lankan government assaults.

The British and French foreign ministers also released a joint statement Wednesday, saying the Tamil Tigers are using Tamil civilians as human shields. The Tigers have been designated a terrorist organization by 32 countries, including the United States and the European Union.

As many as 70,000 people have been killed since the conflict officially began in 1983.

The International Committee of the Red Cross said Monday that it has helped evacuate more than 10,000 sick and injured patients, along with their caregivers, from Putumattalan in rebel-held territory since February.

“These evacuations have saved many lives,” said Morven Murchinson, the Red Cross medical coordinator in Sri Lanka. “It is vital that they continue, because more sick and wounded people are arriving every day at the makeshift medical facilities in Putumattalan.”

The Red Cross said there is an acute shortage of medical supplies in the region, a situation it is working to address.

(CNN) — Sri Lanka’s military said it began a new operation against Tamil rebel forces in the north of the country early Monday, asserting that troops had freed thousands of civilians who had been stranded inside a government-designated safe area.

The army has resumed its assault on the Tamil rebels in northern Sri Lanka. TamilNet, a website linked to the rebels, reported that government troops had started a new ground offensive. One of its correspondents in Vanni described intense shelling, rocket attacks and small-arms fire. Rebel sources said 30 civilians were killed by shelling on Sunday.

Sri Lanka’s government has been fighting the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, in a civil war that has continued for almost 25 years.

According to a statement posted on the Ministry of Defense website, “thousands of civilians” who had been held by LTTE “terrorists” in the government-declared No Fire Zone were rescued in the early hours of Monday, April 20, after troops carrying out a large-scale rescue operation managed to create a safe route for them to leave.

The military said more than 10,000 civilians were attempting to reach government soldiers for protection.

The renewed fighting came after a two-day pause in combat the previous week for the Sinhala and Hindu New Year.

On Thursday, the U.S. State Department urged both the Sri Lankan government and the Tamil Tigers to agree to a cease-fire so civilians could get out of the battle zone.

“We call upon the government and military of Sri Lanka, and the Tamil Tigers, to immediately stop hostilities until the more than 140,000 civilians in the conflict area are safely out,” acting spokesman Robert Wood said in a statement. He added that both sides should immediately resume a humanitarian pause and must honor the right of trapped civilian men, women and children to move freely.

A short halt in fighting, announced by the Sri Lankan government on April 12, enabled the United Nations and aid partners to deliver assistance. However, a later government offensive left civilians caught inside the war zone.

U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and U.N. humanitarian chief John Holmes said the brief pause was not sufficient and have pressed for a longer humanitarian break in the fighting.

Holmes said the most urgent problem was that more than 100,000 people were packed into a “very small pocket of land” measuring roughly five square miles — about twice the size of New York’s Central Park.

“It is a very small area indeed for what we believe is a very large number of people,” Holmes told reporters Wednesday.

The United Nations Children’s Fund, UNICEF, also said overcrowding was a serious issue in camps sheltering people displaced by the conflict. In a statement, the agency said that by Monday about 65,000 displaced people were crowded into camps in Vavuniya, Jaffna and Mannar, and that another 35,000 were expected to arrive within 48 hours.

UNICEF said it was deeply concerned about children trapped amid the intensifying violence and feared that conditions could deteriorate further. The agency requested donations to address the most urgent needs of affected people, including health care, nutrition, clean water, sanitation, protection and education.

The civilians concentrated in the area, most of them Tamils, remain exposed to ongoing attacks by Sri Lankan government forces.

Also on Wednesday, the foreign ministers of Britain and France issued a joint statement saying the Tamil Tigers were using Tamil civilians as human shields.

The LTTE has been listed as a terrorist organization by 32 countries, among them the United States and the European Union.

Since the conflict officially began in 1983, as many as 70,000 people have been killed.

The International Committee of the Red Cross said Monday that since February it had helped evacuate more than 10,000 sick and wounded patients, along with their caregivers, from Putumattalan, an area controlled by the rebels.

“These evacuations have saved many lives,” said Morven Murchinson, the Red Cross medical coordinator in Sri Lanka. “It is vital that they continue, because more sick and wounded people are arriving every day at the makeshift medical facilities in Putumattalan.”

The Red Cross said medical supplies in the area were critically low and that it was working to address the shortage.

counterfactuals.output:
**Sri Lankan army launches renewed northern offensive against Tamil Tiger rebels amid civilian evacuation fears**

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka** — Sri Lankan government forces have launched a renewed offensive against Tamil Tiger rebels in the country’s north, pushing deeper into rebel-held territory as thousands of civilians attempt to flee the fighting, officials and aid groups said.

The military said its troops were advancing on multiple fronts in the northern conflict zone, targeting positions held by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE. Army officials described the operation as part of a final push to dismantle the separatist group’s remaining strongholds.

“Our forces are moving forward and clearing rebel defenses,” a military spokesman said, adding that soldiers were working to open routes for trapped civilians to leave the area.

But humanitarian agencies warned that the renewed fighting has placed civilians at grave risk. The United Nations said it was deeply concerned about reports of heavy shelling near densely populated areas and called on both sides to ensure the safe passage of noncombatants.

Tens of thousands of people are believed to be trapped in the northern war zone, where food, medicine and clean water are in short supply. Aid workers say many families have been displaced multiple times as the front lines shift.

Sri Lankan officials said evacuation corridors had been established and urged civilians to move toward government-controlled areas. The government has accused the Tamil Tigers of using civilians as human shields, a charge the rebels have denied.

The LTTE, which has fought for decades for a separate homeland for Sri Lanka’s ethnic Tamil minority, said government attacks were endangering civilians and called for international pressure to halt the offensive.

The United Nations and several foreign governments have appealed for an immediate pause in the fighting to allow civilians to evacuate and humanitarian supplies to reach those still trapped.

Diplomats from the United States, European Union and regional governments have called for a cease-fire, warning that the conflict could produce a worsening humanitarian crisis if civilians are not protected.

Sri Lanka’s government has resisted international calls for a broad cease-fire, saying any halt in military operations would allow the rebels to regroup. Officials have instead called on the LTTE to surrender and release civilians under its control.

The conflict between Sri Lankan forces and the Tamil Tigers has lasted more than 25 years, killing tens of thousands of people and displacing many more. The latest offensive comes as the government says it is closer than ever to ending the insurgency militarily.

Human rights groups have urged independent access to the conflict zone, saying reliable information remains limited and civilian casualties are difficult to verify.

As fighting continues, aid agencies say the immediate priority is evacuation.

“Civilians must be allowed to leave safely,” one humanitarian official said. “They cannot be caught between advancing troops and retreating rebels.”

counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS REPORT — April 2009 Sri Lanka Conflict**

**Sri Lankan forces press offensive in “No Fire Zone” as civilians remain trapped; UN, UNICEF and Red Cross warn of humanitarian catastrophe**

**Colombo / Vanni, Sri Lanka — April 2009** — Sri Lanka’s military is pressing ahead with its final offensive against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, inside a shrinking coastal strip in the island’s northeast where tens of thousands of civilians are trapped, according to international agencies, aid workers, and Tamil media reports.

The area, designated by the Sri Lankan government as a **“No Fire Zone”**, has become the center of the war’s endgame. Government forces say they are conducting a rescue operation to free civilians being held by the LTTE, while Tamil sources and humanitarian organizations report heavy civilian suffering amid continued fighting, shelling, shortages of food and medicine, and restricted access for aid agencies.

Sri Lankan officials say the LTTE is using civilians as human shields and preventing them from leaving. The LTTE and pro-Tamil outlets, including **TamilNet**, have accused the military of shelling civilian concentrations and medical points inside the No Fire Zone. Independent verification remains extremely limited because journalists and most international observers have been barred from the conflict area.

## Government says operation aims to free civilians

The Sri Lankan government says its troops have pushed the LTTE into a small pocket along the northeastern coast, after months of advances across the Vanni region. Military officials describe the operation as a final humanitarian effort to rescue civilians and defeat the LTTE’s remaining fighters.

Government spokesmen have repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians and have accused the LTTE of firing from civilian areas, holding people by force, and using the No Fire Zone as a defensive shield. Colombo says large numbers of civilians have managed to escape to government-held territory in recent days and are being transferred to screening and displacement camps.

Officials also say the conflict is nearing its conclusion after more than two decades of civil war.

## Civilians trapped in shrinking coastal strip

Humanitarian agencies, however, warn that the situation for civilians inside the conflict zone is dire. The exact number of trapped people is disputed. The Sri Lankan government has offered lower figures, while UN and aid sources have at various points estimated that tens of thousands — and possibly well over 100,000 earlier in the month — were caught in the area.

Those trapped are believed to include large numbers of women, children, the elderly, and wounded civilians. Reports from the area describe severe shortages of food, clean water, shelter, and medical supplies. Makeshift hospitals and medical posts are said to be overwhelmed.

The No Fire Zone, intended as a civilian safe area, has instead become a battlefield as the front line has collapsed into a narrow strip near the coast.

## TamilNet reports mass casualties and shelling claims

TamilNet, a pro-Tamil news website often cited for reports from LTTE-held areas, has claimed that Sri Lankan forces have shelled civilian areas, hospitals, and refugee concentrations inside the No Fire Zone. It has reported large casualty figures and accused the government of carrying out indiscriminate attacks during the final push.

Because access to the battlefield is severely restricted, TamilNet’s casualty claims cannot be independently confirmed. The Sri Lankan government has rejected many such reports as LTTE propaganda, saying the rebels are fabricating or exaggerating civilian casualty numbers to trigger international pressure for a ceasefire.

Still, the persistence of civilian casualty reports has intensified international alarm, especially as UN agencies and the International Committee of the Red Cross have issued increasingly urgent warnings.

## UN warns of “bloodbath” risk

The United Nations has warned that the fighting could result in a catastrophic loss of civilian life if heavy weapons continue to be used in or near densely populated civilian areas.

Senior UN officials have called for an immediate pause in fighting to allow civilians to leave and for humanitarian workers to deliver aid. The UN has also demanded that the LTTE allow civilians to move freely and urged the Sri Lankan government to avoid the use of heavy firepower where civilians are present.

UN officials have described the trapped population as being in extreme danger, with insufficient medical care and rising numbers of wounded. The organization has also expressed concern about conditions in government-run camps receiving people fleeing the conflict zone.

## UNICEF: children at grave risk

UNICEF has warned that children are among the most vulnerable victims of the fighting. The agency has expressed concern over reports of children being killed, injured, separated from families, or trapped without adequate food and medical treatment.

UNICEF has also previously accused the LTTE of recruiting children during the conflict, while urging all parties to protect minors from the fighting. In April 2009, the agency emphasized that children inside the No Fire Zone faced immediate danger from combat, disease, malnutrition, and lack of medical assistance.

## Red Cross says aid access is collapsing

The International Committee of the Red Cross, one of the few international organizations with limited access to the war zone by sea, has warned that the humanitarian situation is rapidly deteriorating.

The ICRC has called for safe passage for civilians and medical evacuations for the wounded. It has described overcrowded medical facilities, shortages of basic supplies, and the growing difficulty of reaching civilians trapped between the Sri Lankan military and LTTE positions.

Red Cross ships have carried some wounded civilians out of the conflict zone, but aid workers say evacuations and deliveries are far below what is needed.

## International pressure mounts

The United States, European Union, United Nations, and human rights groups have called for restraint, humanitarian access, and protection of civilians. International officials have urged both sides to stop actions that endanger noncombatants: the government by avoiding attacks in civilian areas, and the LTTE by allowing civilians to leave.

Sri Lanka has resisted calls for a full ceasefire, arguing that a pause would allow the LTTE leadership to regroup or escape. The government maintains that the war is in its final stage and that ending the LTTE militarily is necessary to bring lasting peace.

Human rights organizations say both sides may be violating international humanitarian law: the LTTE by allegedly holding civilians and firing from populated areas, and government forces if they are using indiscriminate fire in civilian zones.

## Endgame of a decades-long war

The battle marks the apparent final phase of Sri Lanka’s civil war, which began in the early 1980s. The LTTE fought for an independent Tamil state in the north and east, citing discrimination against the Tamil minority. The Sri Lankan government has long designated the LTTE a terrorist organization, accusing it of suicide bombings, assassinations, child recruitment, and attacks on civilians.

By April 2009, the LTTE had lost nearly all territory it once controlled. Its remaining fighters and leadership were believed to be encircled in a narrow coastal pocket, along with a large civilian population.

## Humanitarian crisis deepens as fighting continues

As the offensive continues, the central question remains the fate of civilians trapped inside the No Fire Zone. Aid agencies say urgent access is needed to evacuate the wounded, deliver food and medicine, and allow civilians to flee safely.

With independent reporting blocked and each side accusing the other of manipulating casualty figures, the full scale of the crisis remains unclear. But warnings from the UN, UNICEF, and the Red Cross point to a rapidly escalating humanitarian emergency at the heart of Sri Lanka’s final battlefield.

counterfactuals.output:
**Sri Lanka Fighting Escalates as U.S. Urges Cease-Fire, Civilians Trapped in War Zone**

*Colombo, Sri Lanka* — Fighting between Sri Lankan government forces and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam intensified sharply as the military pressed deeper into the rebels’ remaining territory in the island’s northeast, raising fears for tens of thousands of civilians trapped in the conflict zone.

The Sri Lankan military said its troops were advancing against the LTTE, commonly known as the Tamil Tigers, after months of heavy ground offensives aimed at ending the rebels’ decades-long separatist insurgency. Government officials have described the campaign as a final push to dismantle the LTTE’s remaining strongholds and restore state control over the region.

But aid agencies and human rights groups warned that civilians are paying a devastating price. Reports from the conflict area described artillery fire, shortages of food and medicine, and desperate attempts by families to flee the fighting. Civilian casualties have mounted as combat has moved into densely populated areas, with hospitals and makeshift medical points struggling to treat the wounded under increasingly dangerous conditions.

The U.S. State Department appealed for an immediate cease-fire to allow civilians to leave the combat zone and permit humanitarian workers to deliver urgently needed assistance. American officials urged both the Sri Lankan government and the LTTE to take steps to protect noncombatants, calling for a pause in the fighting and safe passage for those trapped.

International concern has focused in particular on a shrinking area where large numbers of civilians are believed to be caught between advancing government troops and retreating Tiger fighters. The United Nations and humanitarian organizations have repeatedly called for the protection of civilians and warned that conditions inside the war zone are deteriorating rapidly.

Sri Lankan authorities have accused the LTTE of preventing civilians from leaving and using them as human shields, allegations echoed by several international observers. The rebels have denied intentionally endangering civilians, but multiple reports have said Tiger cadres fired on or coerced civilians who tried to escape. The use of civilians to shield military positions has drawn sharp condemnation and complicated efforts to establish humanitarian corridors.

At the same time, the Sri Lankan government has faced criticism over the scale and conduct of its offensive, including allegations that shelling and air or artillery strikes have caused civilian deaths. Officials in Colombo have rejected accusations that the military is deliberately targeting civilians, saying troops are carrying out operations against a militant organization embedded among the population.

Those who manage to flee the fighting face a new crisis in government-run displacement camps. Camps set up to receive displaced Tamils have become overcrowded, with families packed into temporary shelters and dependent on limited supplies of food, clean water and medical care. Aid workers have warned of poor sanitation, disease risks and restrictions on access, saying the camps are struggling to cope with the rapid influx of civilians.

The government says the screening of displaced people is necessary to identify LTTE fighters hiding among civilians. However, rights groups have urged authorities to ensure freedom of movement, family reunification and full humanitarian access, arguing that displaced civilians should not be treated as security threats.

The latest escalation marks one of the most intense phases of Sri Lanka’s long civil war, which began after Tamil militants took up arms demanding an independent homeland for the Tamil minority in the north and east. The LTTE, once one of the world’s most powerful guerrilla organizations, has been accused of suicide bombings, political assassinations, forced recruitment and attacks on civilians. The Sri Lankan government has vowed to eliminate the group militarily.

As the battlefield narrows, diplomatic pressure is growing. The United States, United Nations and other international actors have urged an immediate humanitarian pause, warning that without a cease-fire the civilian death toll could rise further. For thousands of families trapped in the fighting or confined to overcrowded camps, the end of the war may still bring little immediate relief.
